subject: film
title: The Iranian New Wave, 1962 to 2000
dek: In 1969 a film about a villager who loses his cow, and then his mind, was banned by the Shah's government, smuggled to Venice, and won a critics' prize. Twenty-eight years later an Iranian film shared the Palme d'Or at Cannes. Between those two moments came a revolution, an eight-year war, a strict new code of what could be shown on screen, and two generations of filmmakers — Farrokhzad, Mehrjui, Beyzaie, Kiarostami, Makhmalbaf, Bani-Etemad, Panahi and many others — who turned plain stories about children, villages and ordinary people into some of the most admired films in the world. This lesson covers both waves, the people and films, how censorship shaped the style, and what the rest of world cinema was doing at the same time.
era: c. 1962 to 2000: precursors in the 1960s, a first wave from 1969 to the 1979 revolution, and a second wave from the late 1980s, with a short look at what followed
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English Wikipedia articles on the Iranian New Wave, the cinema of Iran, the films and the directors, in festival records from Cannes, Venice, Berlin and Locarno, and in reporting by The Guardian, The Independent, MERIP and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. Numbers that are disputed, such as the death toll of the Cinema Rex fire, are given as a range. Where a detail could not be checked, it was left out. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Filmfarsi fills the cinemas
timeline.detail: Popular Iranian cinema is dominated by Filmfarsi: song-and-dance melodramas and tough-guy films modelled on Hollywood and Indian cinema, under heavy Pahlavi-era censorship.

timeline.label: The House Is Black
timeline.detail: The poet Forough Farrokhzad films a 20-minute documentary at the Bababaghi leper colony near Tabriz, produced by Ebrahim Golestan's studio. In 1963 it wins the documentary grand prize at the Oberhausen short film festival in West Germany.

timeline.label: Precursors
timeline.detail: Farrokh Ghaffari's Night of the Hunchback (1964), Golestan's Brick and Mirror (1965) and Fereydoun Rahnema's Siavash in Persepolis (1967) point toward a more serious, modern Iranian cinema.

timeline.label: Kanoon is founded
timeline.detail: The Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults, known as Kanoon, is set up under the patronage of Empress Farah Pahlavi, first to build libraries for children.

timeline.label: The Cow and Qeysar
timeline.detail: Dariush Mehrjui's The Cow and Masoud Kimiai's Qeysar are released. Qeysar modernises the tough-guy film; The Cow becomes the founding film of the new wave.

timeline.label: Bread and Alley
timeline.detail: Abbas Kiarostami helps set up Kanoon's film department. Its first production is his twelve-minute short The Bread and Alley, about a schoolboy and a dog.

timeline.label: The Cow wins at Venice
timeline.detail: Banned at home for its picture of rural poverty, The Cow is smuggled out and wins the FIPRESCI critics' prize at the Venice Film Festival. Bahram Beyzaie makes his first feature, Downpour.

timeline.label: Shahid-Saless
timeline.detail: Sohrab Shahid-Saless makes A Simple Event (1973) and Still Life (1974), which wins a Silver Bear at the Berlin festival.

timeline.label: The Cinema Rex fire
timeline.detail: On 19 August, during a screening of Kimiai's The Deer, arsonists bar the doors of the Cinema Rex in Abadan and set it alight, killing between 377 and 470 people. It becomes a turning point in the revolution.

timeline.label: Revolution
timeline.detail: The Shah leaves and the Islamic Republic is founded. Cinema's future is uncertain; Ayatollah Khomeini is reported to have admired The Cow, which is often credited with helping cinema survive.

timeline.label: Iran–Iraq War
timeline.detail: An eight-year war shapes the decade. Under Mohammad Khatami at the Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance, a state system of funding, script approval and screening permits takes shape.

timeline.label: Farabi and Fajr
timeline.detail: The Farabi Cinema Foundation is set up to rebuild the industry, and the Fajr Film Festival begins to be held every February in Tehran.

timeline.label: Where Is the Friend's House?
timeline.detail: Kiarostami's film about a boy trying to return a classmate's notebook begins what critics later call the Koker trilogy. Makhmalbaf releases The Cyclist.

timeline.label: Bashu reaches audiences
timeline.detail: Beyzaie's Bashu, the Little Stranger, made in 1986, is finally released. Mehrjui's Hamoun appears the same year.

timeline.label: Close-Up
timeline.detail: Kiarostami's Close-Up restages the real case of Hossein Sabzian, who pretended to be Makhmalbaf. On 20 June the Manjil–Rudbar earthquake kills about 40,000 people, the background to Kiarostami's next two Koker films.

timeline.label: Nargess
timeline.detail: Rakhshan Bani-Etemad becomes the first woman to win the best director award at the Fajr Film Festival.

timeline.label: The White Balloon
timeline.detail: Jafar Panahi's debut wins the Caméra d'Or at Cannes, the first major Cannes award for an Iranian film.

timeline.label: Taste of Cherry
timeline.detail: Kiarostami's Taste of Cherry shares the Palme d'Or with Shohei Imamura's The Eel. Mohammad Khatami is elected president in May.

timeline.label: The Apple; Children of Heaven
timeline.detail: Samira Makhmalbaf, at 17, makes her first feature, The Apple. Majid Majidi's Children of Heaven becomes the first Iranian film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

timeline.label: The Circle and The Day I Became a Woman
timeline.detail: Panahi's The Circle, about women in Tehran, wins the Golden Lion at Venice and is banned in Iran. Marzieh Meshkini's The Day I Became a Woman wins awards at the same festival.

fun_fact.title: The most famous kiss in Iranian cinema was on a cheek
fun_fact.text: Taste of Cherry almost missed Cannes in 1997: the Ministry of Islamic Guidance held back its export permit so long that the reels arrived after the festival had begun. When the film then shared the Palme d'Or — the first for an Iranian film — Catherine Deneuve presented the prize, and she and Kiarostami exchanged a polite kiss on the cheek. In France that was ordinary manners. In Iran, conservative critics treated a public kiss with a woman who was not his wife as an offence, the scandal overshadowed the prize, and when Kiarostami flew home he was taken through customs and out a side door to avoid protesters waiting at the airport.

sections.title: Filmfarsi, a poet with a camera, and the 1960s

blocks.text: Cinema reached Iran early. In 1900 Mozaffar ad-Din Shah saw the cinematograph in France and had his court photographer buy one, and Tehran had cinemas within a few years. But by the 1950s and 1960s the films most Iranians actually watched belonged to what critics call Filmfarsi: cheaply made melodramas, comedies and tough-guy stories with songs and dances, borrowing freely from Hollywood and Indian cinema. Censorship under the Pahlavi monarchy was strict, and films that showed poverty, corruption or politics in a serious way had a hard time getting made or shown.

The film that people usually point to as the seed of something different was not a feature at all. In 1962 Forough Farrokhzad, already one of the most important and most controversial poets in Persian, went to the Bababaghi leper colony near Tabriz with a small crew from Ebrahim Golestan's studio. The result, The House Is Black, is about twenty minutes long. It shows the patients plainly — eating, praying, going to school, getting married — and sets the images against Farrokhzad's own voice reading from the Old Testament, the Quran and her own poetry. In 1963 it won the documentary grand prize at the International Short Film Festival Oberhausen in West Germany, the same festival where, a year earlier, young German filmmakers had issued the Oberhausen Manifesto that this site covered in the New German Cinema lesson. Farrokhzad died in a car accident in February 1967, at 32.

Other precursors followed in feature films. Farrokh Ghaffari's Night of the Hunchback (1964) was a dark comedy set in Tehran. Golestan's Brick and Mirror (1965), in which a taxi driver finds an abandoned baby in his cab, looked at the city at night with a seriousness Filmfarsi did not have. Fereydoun Rahnema's Siavash in Persepolis (1967) was a modernist retelling of an episode from the Shahnameh. None of these was a box-office hit, but together they showed that another kind of Iranian film was possible.

sections.title: 1969: The Cow, Qeysar, and a decade of new films

blocks.text: The year usually given for the start of the Iranian New Wave is 1969, when two very different films came out. Masoud Kimiai's Qeysar, about a young man who takes revenge for the rape of his sister and the murder of his brother, was a huge popular success. It gave new energy to the jaheli or tough-guy film, a popular genre. Dariush Mehrjui's The Cow went the other way. Mehrjui had studied at UCLA, first cinema and then philosophy, and he adapted the film from a story by the writer Gholam-Hossein Sa'edi. It is set in a poor village, in black and white. Hassan, played by Ezzatollah Entezami, owns the only cow in the village and loves it more than anything. While he is away, the cow dies. The villagers bury it and tell him it ran away, and Hassan slowly comes to believe that he himself is the cow.

The government banned The Cow because of the way it showed rural poverty, which did not fit the image of a modernising Iran that the Shah's government wanted to project. A print was smuggled out of the country, and in 1971 the film won the FIPRESCI critics' prize at the Venice Film Festival. That outside recognition, and the eventual release at home, made it the founding film of the movement. Historians note that the new wave never had a manifesto or a magazine of its own, and its directors came from different backgrounds and had different styles, so it is better described as a moment than as an organised school.

Through the 1970s that moment produced a remarkable list of films. Nasser Taghvai's Tranquility in the Presence of Others was banned and then released in a censored version. Bahram Beyzaie, a playwright and scholar of Persian theatre, made his first feature, Downpour, in 1971, about a teacher who arrives in a poor Tehran neighbourhood; critics still rank it among the best Iranian films. Sohrab Shahid-Saless made A Simple Event (1973), about a ten-year-old boy in a small town whose father smuggles fish and whose mother is ill, and Still Life (1974), about an old railway signalman, which won a Silver Bear at the Berlin festival. His long, quiet takes of everyday life would influence later Iranian directors. Shahid-Saless left for West Germany in 1976 and worked there for the rest of his career; he died in Chicago in 1998.

An unexpected home for new filmmaking was Kanoon, the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults. It was founded in 1965 under the patronage of Empress Farah Pahlavi, first to build libraries for children. Under its co-director Firooz Shirvanloo it drew in illustrators, graphic designers, animators and filmmakers, and gave them unusual creative freedom. In 1970 Abbas Kiarostami, then a graphic designer, helped start its film department. Its first production was his twelve-minute The Bread and Alley, in which a boy carrying bread home has to get past a barking dog. Kanoon would go on to produce many of Kiarostami's films, and its children's cinema became one of the bridges across the revolution.

sections.title: The Cinema Rex fire, the revolution, and new rules

blocks.text: Cinemas were among the targets of the revolutionary movement of 1978, because many religious opponents of the Shah saw them as symbols of Western immorality. The worst attack happened on 19 August 1978 in the oil city of Abadan. During an evening screening of Kimiai's The Deer, four men barred the doors of the Cinema Rex and set it on fire. Between 377 and 470 people died; the exact figure is still disputed. At the time many protesters blamed SAVAK, the Shah's secret police, and the fire increased anger against the government. Later trials and investigations pointed instead to a radical Islamist group, and Hossein Takbalizadeh was identified as one of the four men who set the fire.

After the Shah left in January 1979 and the Islamic Republic was established, it was not obvious that cinema would survive at all. One story often told is that Ayatollah Khomeini had seen and admired The Cow, and that this helped persuade the new leadership that film could serve good purposes rather than only corrupt ones. Many people from the old industry left the country or stopped working. Mehrjui went to Paris in 1981 and stayed several years.

In the 1980s the new state built its own system. Mohammad Khatami became minister of culture and Islamic guidance in 1982. The Farabi Cinema Foundation was set up in 1983 to support production, and the Fajr Film Festival has been held in Tehran every February since 1983. Scripts, productions and final cuts needed approval, and there was a code of conduct for what could be shown. Actresses had to wear the hijab and loose clothing on screen at all times, even in scenes set inside a home or in bed, where real Iranian women did not cover their hair. Men and women who were not related in real life could not touch, even when they were playing husband and wife. Women could not sing or dance on screen. All of this took place during the Iran–Iraq War, which lasted from 1980 to 1988 and killed hundreds of thousands of people.

items: Children as main characters. Stories about children avoided many of the problems of showing adult men and women together, and children could move between homes and streets in a way adults on screen could not. Kanoon's experience in children's film helped here.

Real places and non-professional actors. Many films were shot in villages and city streets with local people playing roles close to their own lives, a method critics often compared to Italian Neorealism.

Long takes and simple stories. A search for a notebook, a goldfish, a pair of shoes or a balloon could carry a whole film, and the larger subjects — poverty, war, the position of women — sat in the background.
Films about film. Several directors began to put the making of the film itself on screen, blurring the line between documentary and fiction.

sections.title: From the late 1980s: the films the world noticed

blocks.text: By the late 1980s a second wave had formed, mixing veterans of the 1970s with new directors who had come of age during the revolution. Beyzaie's Bashu, the Little Stranger, made in 1986 but held back until 1989, tells of an Afro-Iranian Arab boy from Khuzestan in the south whose parents are killed in a bombing raid in the war. He escapes on a cargo truck and ends up in the green Caspian north. A Gilak farming woman named Na'i, played by Susan Taslimi, takes him in although he speaks Arabic and she speaks Gilaki and her neighbours call him a stranger. It was the first Iranian film to use the northern Gilaki language seriously rather than for comic relief, and it quietly questions the idea of a single Iranian identity and puts a strong, independent woman at its centre. Mehrjui, back from Paris, made The Tenants (1987) and Hamoun (1989), a portrait of an intellectual whose life is falling apart.

Mohsen Makhmalbaf took a different road into cinema. Born in Tehran in 1957, he joined a militant group fighting the Shah at 15, was imprisoned at 17 for stabbing a policeman, and was released after five years in the wake of the revolution. He began making films with a strongly religious outlook and then moved toward more open, questioning work. The Cyclist (1987) follows an Afghan refugee in Iran who agrees to ride a bicycle in circles for days without stopping to pay for his wife's hospital care. Salaam Cinema (1995) films the open auditions for one of his own films. A Moment of Innocence (1996) restages an episode from his own youth, the stabbing of the policeman, with the real policeman taking part. Gabbeh (1996) is a colourful story woven around a nomadic tribe's carpets. Kandahar (2001) is set in Afghanistan just before 11 September.

Many of the strongest films of these years were made by women. Rakhshan Bani-Etemad, born in Tehran in 1954, began in documentary and drew her fiction from that work. Nargess (1991), about a young couple and an older woman in a poor Tehran neighbourhood, made her the first woman to win the best director prize at the Fajr festival. The Blue-Veiled (1995) won a Bronze Leopard at Locarno, and The May Lady (1998) and Under the Skin of the City (2001) followed. Tahmineh Milani's Two Women (1999) contrasted the lives of two university friends; in 2001 she was jailed over her film The Hidden Half, even though it had been approved by the reformist government. Samira Makhmalbaf, Mohsen's daughter, directed her first feature, The Apple, at 17 in 1998, about two girls kept indoors by their father for years, with the real family playing themselves. Her Blackboards (2000) won the Jury Prize at Cannes. Marzieh Meshkini's The Day I Became a Woman (2000), in three stories about a girl, a young wife and an old woman, won awards at Venice. Readers of this site's feminist film theory lesson will recognise the questions these films raise about who looks, who is looked at, and what can be shown.

Majid Majidi's Children of Heaven (1997), about a brother and sister who share one pair of shoes after the boy loses hers, became the first Iranian film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film; it lost to Roberto Benigni's Life Is Beautiful. Jafar Panahi, who had worked as Kiarostami's assistant, made The White Balloon (1995), written by Kiarostami, in which a little girl in Tehran tries to buy a goldfish for the Persian New Year, Nowruz. It won the Caméra d'Or at Cannes. His The Mirror (1997) won the Golden Leopard at Locarno. The Circle (2000) follows a chain of women — some just released from prison — through one day in Tehran and shows how little room the law and the street leave them. It won the Golden Lion at Venice and was banned in Iran. Other names to know from these years include Amir Naderi, whose The Runner followed a boy surviving alone in a southern port city, and Bahman Ghobadi, whose Kurdish-language A Time for Drunken Horses, about orphaned children on the Iran–Iraq border, shared the Caméra d'Or at Cannes in 2000.

sections.title: Kiarostami: the Koker films, Close-Up and Taste of Cherry

blocks.text: Abbas Kiarostami (1940–2016) is the director most closely identified with the Iranian New Wave abroad. After two decades of shorts and features for Kanoon, he made Where Is the Friend's House? in 1987. A schoolboy, Ahmad, realises he has taken his classmate's notebook home by mistake; the teacher has warned the classmate he will be expelled if he does not do his homework in it again. Ahmad spends the evening walking from his village, Koker, to the next village and back, trying to find the friend's house, while the adults around him ignore what he is saying. It is a very simple film, and also a careful study of how adults fail to listen to children.

Close-Up (1990) came from a newspaper story. Hossein Sabzian, a poor print-shop worker who loved films, was riding a bus with the published screenplay of Makhmalbaf's The Cyclist when he told the woman next to him that he was Makhmalbaf. For about two weeks he visited her family, the Ahankhahs, promising to cast them in his next film, until a journalist confirmed he was an impostor and he was arrested. Kiarostami persuaded Sabzian, the family, and the journalist to re-enact the events as themselves, filmed Sabzian's real trial, and arranged for the real Makhmalbaf to meet him on his release. The two men ride to the family's house on a motorbike and stop to buy flowers. In the 2022 Sight and Sound critics' poll it was ranked the 17th greatest film ever made.

On 20 June 1990 the Manjil–Rudbar earthquake struck northern Iran and killed about 40,000 people. Kiarostami went back to the region to look for the boys from his earlier film. And Life Goes On (1992) follows a director and his son driving through the wreckage. Through the Olive Trees (1994) is about the making of a scene from the previous film, and about the young man who keeps asking the young woman playing opposite him to marry him. Critics call the three films the Koker trilogy, and each one steps back from the one before, until the films are partly about their own making.

Taste of Cherry (1997) follows Mr Badii, a middle-aged man driving around the dusty hills outside Tehran, looking for someone who will agree, for money, to throw earth over him in a grave he has dug, after he has taken an overdose. A young Kurdish soldier runs away, an Afghan seminarian refuses on religious grounds, and an older Azeri taxidermist, who needs money for his sick child, agrees but tries to talk him out of it, telling him how the taste of mulberries once changed his own mind about dying. Suicide was a taboo subject in the Islamic Republic, and the film was initially refused permission to leave the country. At the end, after the screen goes dark, the film cuts to Kiarostami and his crew on the same hill in daylight, with the lead actor alive and wandering among them. It shared the Palme d'Or with Shohei Imamura's The Eel. Kiarostami's later films include The Wind Will Carry Us (1999), Ten (2002), shot entirely inside a car driven by a divorced woman in Tehran, and Certified Copy (2010), made in Italy. He died in 2016.

Iranian filmmakers worked under rules that told them what they could not show, and many of them made that limit part of their style: children instead of couples, long shots from a car instead of intimate scenes, a story about a notebook that is really about how adults treat children. Think about a time you had to say something important under a restriction — at work, in a family, or online. Did the limit make what you said weaker, or did it force you to find a sharper way to say it?

sections.title: What else was happening at the same time

blocks.text: The first wave sat in the middle of the worldwide wave of new cinemas that this site has followed. The Cow (1969) appeared a year after the Prague Spring ended the Czechoslovak New Wave, while Brazil's Cinema Novo and the New German Cinema were at their height and New Hollywood was beginning in the United States. Like several of these movements, the Iranian new wave was a reaction against a commercial cinema that ignored ordinary life, and it was strongly shaped by Italian Neorealism, whose methods — real locations, non-professional actors, stories of the poor — Iranian directors adapted to their own country.

The second wave overlapped with a great period for Chinese-language film. Hou Hsiao-hsien's A City of Sadness, the first major film to deal with the 228 Incident, won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1989, the year Bashu was released, and Tsai Ming-liang's Vive L'Amour won the Golden Lion in 1994. In mainland China, the Fifth Generation's Farewell My Concubine shared the Palme d'Or in 1993. At the 1997 Cannes festival where Taste of Cherry won, Wong Kar-wai won best director for Happy Together, the same year Takeshi Kitano's Hana-bi won the Golden Lion. In Denmark, Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg launched Dogme 95 in 1995, a set of rules that banned studio sets and added music. It is worth comparing: the Danish directors chose their restrictions as an artistic game, while Iranian directors had theirs imposed by the state, and both groups ended up with films of handheld realism and plain storytelling.

Iranian cinema did not stop at the end of the 1990s, but its situation changed. Asghar Farhadi worked within the system and made tightly written dramas of middle-class life. A Separation won the Golden Bear in 2011 and became the first Iranian film to win the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film; The Salesman won the same Oscar in 2017. Other directors made films without permission and sent them abroad. In 2010 Jafar Panahi was sentenced to six years in prison and a twenty-year ban on filmmaking for 'propaganda against the Islamic Republic'. He kept working anyway, in This Is Not a Film (2011), Taxi (2015), which won the Golden Bear, and No Bears (2022). In 2025 It Was Just an Accident won the Palme d'Or, making him one of only four directors to win the top prizes at Cannes, Berlin and Venice.

The generation that founded the new wave has now passed. Kiarostami died in 2016. Dariush Mehrjui and his wife, Vahideh Mohammadifar, were found stabbed to death in their home near Tehran on 14 October 2023. Bahram Beyzaie, who had left Iran in 2010 to teach at Stanford University, died in Palo Alto on 26 December 2025, his 87th birthday. The questions their films raised about women's lives in particular returned to the streets in the Woman, Life, Freedom protests that followed the death of Mahsa Jina Amini in police custody in 2022. If you watch only one film from this lesson, try The House Is Black; if you have time for a second, make it Close-Up.

The war between Iran and Iraq from 1980 to 1988, which killed hundreds of thousands of people.
Iranian minister of culture from 1982, later a reformist president elected in 1997.

glossary.term: Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance
glossary.explain: The Iranian ministry that licenses and censors films.
A state-backed body set up in 1983 to rebuild and support Iranian film production.
Iran's main film festival, held in Tehran every February since 1983.
Islamic head covering and modest dress; Iranian films after 1979 must show actresses wearing it at all times, even in scenes at home.
The post-war Italian movement of real locations, non-professional actors and stories of ordinary people, a strong influence on Iranian directors.
Bahram Beyzaie's 1986 film, released in 1989, about a war-orphaned boy from the south taken in by a woman in the north.
Iranian actress who played Na'i in Bashu, the Little Stranger.
Dariush Mehrjui's 1987 comedy.
Dariush Mehrjui's 1989 film about an intellectual whose life falls apart.
Iranian director born in 1957, maker of The Cyclist, A Moment of Innocence, Gabbeh and Kandahar.
Mohsen Makhmalbaf's 1987 film about an Afghan refugee who rides a bicycle for days to pay for his wife's care.
Mohsen Makhmalbaf's 1995 film about open auditions for one of his films.
Mohsen Makhmalbaf's 1996 film restaging his own youthful stabbing of a policeman, with the real policeman taking part.
Mohsen Makhmalbaf's 1996 film woven around a nomadic tribe's carpets.
Mohsen Makhmalbaf's 2001 film set in Afghanistan just before 11 September.
Iranian director born in 1954, first woman to win best director at the Fajr festival, for Nargess (1991).
Rakhshan Bani-Etemad's 1991 film set in a poor Tehran neighbourhood.
Rakhshan Bani-Etemad's 1995 film, winner of a Bronze Leopard at Locarno.
Rakhshan Bani-Etemad's 1998 film about a divorced documentary filmmaker and her son.

glossary.term: Under the Skin of the City
glossary.explain: Rakhshan Bani-Etemad's 2001 film about a working woman and her family in Tehran.
Iranian director of Two Women (1999), jailed in 2001 over her film The Hidden Half.
Tahmineh Milani's 1999 film about the different lives of two university friends.
Tahmineh Milani's 2001 film about a former leftist student, for which she was jailed.
Iranian director, born in 1980, who made The Apple at 17 and won the Cannes Jury Prize for Blackboards (2000).
Samira Makhmalbaf's 1998 debut about two girls kept indoors by their father, played by the real family.
Samira Makhmalbaf's 2000 film about teachers carrying blackboards through Kurdish border mountains; Jury Prize at Cannes.
Iranian director whose The Day I Became a Woman (2000) won awards at Venice.

glossary.term: The Day I Became a Woman
glossary.explain: Marzieh Meshkini's 2000 film in three stories about a girl, a young wife and an old woman.
Iranian director of Children of Heaven (1997).
Majid Majidi's 1997 film about a brother and sister sharing one pair of shoes, the first Iranian film nominated for the foreign-language Oscar.
Iranian director of The White Balloon, The Mirror, The Circle, Taxi and It Was Just an Accident; banned from filmmaking in 2010.
Jafar Panahi's 1995 debut about a girl trying to buy a goldfish for Nowruz; Caméra d'Or at Cannes.
The Persian New Year, celebrated at the spring equinox.
The Cannes prize for the best first feature film.
Jafar Panahi's 1997 film, winner of the Golden Leopard at Locarno.
A film festival in Switzerland whose top prize is the Golden Leopard.
Jafar Panahi's 2000 film about women in Tehran; Golden Lion at Venice, banned in Iran.
Iranian director associated with Kanoon, maker of The Runner.
Amir Naderi's film about a boy surviving alone in a southern Iranian port city.
Kurdish Iranian director of A Time for Drunken Horses (2000).
Bahman Ghobadi's 2000 film about Kurdish children on the Iran–Iraq border.
Kiarostami's 1987 film about a boy trying to return a classmate's notebook; the first Koker film.
Kiarostami's Where Is the Friend's House? (1987), And Life Goes On (1992) and Through the Olive Trees (1994), linked by the village of Koker.
Kiarostami's 1990 film in which the real people in the Sabzian impostor case re-enact it.
The print-shop worker who pretended to be Mohsen Makhmalbaf and then played himself in Close-Up.
The earthquake of 20 June 1990 in northern Iran that killed about 40,000 people.
Kiarostami's 1992 film about a director searching the earthquake zone.
Kiarostami's 1994 film about the making of a scene from And Life Goes On.
Kiarostami's 1997 film about a man seeking someone to bury him; co-winner of the Palme d'Or.
The top prize of the Cannes Film Festival.
Japanese director whose The Eel shared the 1997 Palme d'Or with Taste of Cherry.
Shohei Imamura's 1997 film, co-winner of the Palme d'Or.
French actress who presented the Palme d'Or to Kiarostami in 1997.
Kiarostami's 1999 film about a media crew waiting in a Kurdish village.
Kiarostami's 2002 film shot entirely inside a car driven by a divorced woman in Tehran.
Kiarostami's 2010 film made in Italy.
The British Film Institute's magazine, whose once-a-decade poll ranks the greatest films.
Taiwanese director of A City of Sadness (1989).
Hou Hsiao-hsien's 1989 film about the 228 Incident; Golden Lion at Venice.
Malaysian-born Taiwanese director whose Vive L'Amour won the Golden Lion in 1994.
Chen Kaige's 1993 film, co-winner of the Palme d'Or.
Hong Kong director who won best director at Cannes in 1997 for Happy Together.
Japanese director whose Hana-bi won the Golden Lion in 1997.
A Danish film movement launched in 1995 by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg with strict rules against sets and added music.
Iranian director of A Separation (2011) and The Salesman (2016), both winners of the foreign-language Oscar.
Asghar Farhadi's 2011 film, winner of the Golden Bear and the first Iranian Oscar for foreign-language film.
Jafar Panahi's 2025 film, winner of the Palme d'Or.
The protest movement in Iran that followed the death of Mahsa Jina Amini in police custody in 2022.
A young Kurdish Iranian woman whose death in morality-police custody in September 2022 set off nationwide protests.
